blocks.title: 1. Linear, Constant, and Identity Functions
teacherCues: Ask: 'What is the simplest type of function and what does its graph look like?'
Show that $ f(x) = ax + b $ is a line with slope $ a $ and $ y $-intercept $ b $.

discoveryHook.scenario: A plumber charges a flat fee of $50 plus $60 per hour. The total cost is $ f(x) = 60x + 50 $—a [[kw:linear function]]. The graph is a straight line. The simplest linear functions are the constant function $ f(x) = c $ (a horizontal line) and the identity function $ f(x) = x $ (a line through the origin with slope 1).

explanation: A [[kw:linear function]] has the form $ f(x) = ax + b $, where $ a $ is the slope and $ b $ is the $ y $-intercept.
Domain: all real numbers $ (-\infty, \infty) $. Range: all real numbers when $ a \neq 0 $.
Special linear functions: the [[kw:constant function]] $ f(x) = c $ (horizontal line, slope 0), and the [[kw:identity function]] $ f(x) = x $ (slope 1, passes through origin).
A linear function is increasing when $ a > 0 $, decreasing when $ a < 0 $, and constant when $ a = 0 $.
[[imp: The graph of any linear function is a straight line.]]

visuals.title: Special Linear Functions

rows.3: Slope 1, domain and range all reals

visuals.caption: All linear functions share a straight-line graph.

formulaCard.title: Linear Functions
notes: Write using point-slope form if given two points.

examples.title: A – Write a linear function from two values
examples.prompt: Write the linear function $ f $ for which $ f(1) = 3 $ and $ f(4) = 0 $.
steps: Use point-slope with $ (1,3) $: $ y - 3 = -1(x - 1) $ → $ y = -x + 4 $.

examples.title: B – Why is a constant function also linear?
examples.prompt: Explain why $ f(x) = 5 $ is considered a linear function even though its graph is a horizontal line.
examples.peerPrompt: Think about the general form $ f(x) = ax + b $.
steps: The general linear form is $ f(x) = ax + b $.
For $ f(x) = 5 $, we can write $ f(x) = 0 \cdot x + 5 $, so $ a = 0 $ and $ b = 5 $.
It is still a polynomial of degree 1 (or 0), and its graph is a straight line (horizontal).
So it fits the definition of a linear function.

examples.title: C – Identify slope and intercept
examples.prompt: For $ f(x) = -2x + 6 $, state the slope, $ y $-intercept, and whether it is increasing or decreasing.
steps: Slope $ m = -2 $, $ y $-intercept $ (0,6) $.
Since $ m < 0 $, the function is decreasing.
Graph falls from left to right.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: Don't confuse 'linear function' with 'line.' A vertical line $ x = a $ is NOT a function. [[imp: Linear functions can be written as $ f(x) = ax + b $, which always passes the vertical line test.]]

questions.prompt: A function of the form $ f(x) = ax + b $ is called a ___ function.
What is the slope of the identity function $ f(x) = x $? (number only)
If $ f $ is linear with $ f(2)=5 $ and $ f(6)=13 $, find the slope $ m $. (number only)

challengeCorner.prompt: Write the linear function $ f $ for which $ f(-2)=6 $ and $ f(4)= -9 $.

blocks.title: 2. Squaring, Cubic, and Power Functions
teacherCues: Ask: 'What shape does $ y = x^2 $ have? What about $ y = x^3 $?'
Show graphs side by side and note symmetry.

discoveryHook.scenario: The path of a ball thrown upward is a parabola—the graph of a [[kw:squaring function]] $ f(x) = x^2 $. But the volume of a cube with side $ x $ is $ V(x) = x^3 $, a [[kw:cubic function]]. These are two fundamental building blocks, or [[kw:parent functions]], in algebra.

explanation: The [[kw:squaring function]] $ f(x) = x^2 $ has domain all real numbers, range $ [0, \infty) $. It is even, symmetric about the $ y $-axis. It decreases on $ (-\infty, 0) $ and increases on $ (0, \infty) $, with a relative (and absolute) minimum at $ (0,0) $.

The [[kw:cubic function]] $ f(x) = x^3 $ has domain and range all real numbers. It is odd, symmetric about the origin. It is increasing on $ (-\infty, \infty) $, with an inflection point at $ (0,0) $.
These are both [[kw:parent functions]]—the simplest forms of polynomial functions.

visuals.title: Squaring vs. Cubic Functions
visuals.caption: Both pass through the origin but have very different shapes.

formulaCard.title: Squaring & Cubic Parent Functions
notes: $ x^2 $: U-shaped parabola, minimum at vertex.

examples.title: A – Graph and describe $ f(x) = x^2 - 1 $
examples.prompt: How does the graph of $ f(x) = x^2 - 1 $ differ from the parent $ y = x^2 $?
steps: It is the parent graph shifted down 1 unit.
Still even, symmetric about $ y $-axis, minimum at $ (0,-1) $.

examples.title: B – Even vs. odd powers
examples.prompt: Explain why $ f(x) = x^4 $ behaves similarly to $ x^2 $ (even), while $ x^5 $ behaves like $ x^3 $ (odd).
examples.peerPrompt: Think about what happens when you plug in negative values.
steps: For even powers, $ (-x)^n = x^n $, so the function is even and symmetric about the $ y $-axis.
For odd powers, $ (-x)^n = -x^n $, so the function is odd and symmetric about the origin.
The general shape of the graph depends on whether the highest power is even or odd.

examples.title: C – Identify parent function
examples.prompt: What parent function does $ g(x) = (x-2)^3 + 4 $ come from?
steps: The parent is the cubic function $ f(x) = x^3 $.
The graph is shifted right 2 and up 4.
Still increasing everywhere, odd symmetry is lost due to shift.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: $ f(x) = x^3 $ is increasing everywhere, even though it flattens near the origin. [[imp: The function never decreases; it just slows down briefly at $ x=0 $.]]

questions.prompt: The graph of $ f(x) = x^2 $ is a U-shaped curve called a ___.
Is $ f(x) = x^3 $ even, odd, or neither?
What is the minimum value of $ f(x) = x^2 $? (number only)

challengeCorner.prompt: Determine the intervals where $ f(x) = -x^2 + 4 $ is increasing and decreasing.
hints: Vertex at $ (0,4) $; increases to the left, decreases to the right.

blocks.title: 3. Square Root and Reciprocal Functions
teacherCues: Ask: 'What happens when you take the square root of $ x $? What about its reciprocal?'
Graph both and note domain restrictions.

discoveryHook.scenario: The time to fall from a height $ h $ is proportional to $ \sqrt{h} $—a [[kw:square root function]]. The intensity of light decreases as $ 1/d^2 $, which is related to the [[kw:reciprocal function]] $ f(x) = 1/x $. Both have restricted domains and characteristic shapes.

explanation: The [[kw:square root function]] $ f(x) = \sqrt{x} $ has domain $ [0, \infty) $ and range $ [0, \infty) $. It increases on $ (0, \infty) $, passes through $ (0,0) $, and is neither even nor odd.

The [[kw:reciprocal function]] $ f(x) = \frac{1}{x} $ has domain and range $ (-\infty, 0) \cup (0, \infty) $. It is odd, symmetric about the origin. It decreases on $ (-\infty, 0) $ and $ (0, \infty) $ separately, with vertical and horizontal asymptotes at $ x=0 $ and $ y=0 $.
Both are parent functions with domain restrictions.
[[imp: The square root function only takes non-negative inputs; the reciprocal function is undefined at $ x=0 $.]]

visuals.title: Square Root and Reciprocal Functions
visuals.caption: Both have restricted domains; reciprocal function has asymptotes.

formulaCard.title: Square Root & Reciprocal
notes: Both are building blocks for more complex functions.

examples.title: A – Evaluate and graph $ \sqrt{x} $
examples.prompt: Find $ f(0), f(1), f(4), f(9) $ for $ f(x) = \sqrt{x} $ and sketch the graph.
steps: The graph starts at $ (0,0) $, curves upward, getting flatter as $ x $ increases.
Domain: $ [0,\infty) $; range: $ [0,\infty) $.

examples.title: B – Why does $ 1/x $ have no intercepts?
examples.prompt: Explain why the reciprocal function $ f(x) = \frac{1}{x} $ has no $ x $- or $ y $-intercepts.
examples.peerPrompt: Think about what it would mean for the numerator or denominator to be zero.
steps: For a $ y $-intercept, $ x=0 $, but $ f(0) = 1/0 $ is undefined, so no $ y $-intercept.
For an $ x $-intercept, $ f(x)=0 $ would mean $ 1/x = 0 $, which has no solution (a nonzero constant divided by something cannot be zero).
The graph approaches but never touches either axis.

examples.title: C – Domain of a shifted reciprocal
steps: The denominator $ x-2 $ cannot be zero.
So $ x \neq 2 $.
Domain: $ (-\infty, 2) \cup (2, \infty) $.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: The reciprocal function $ 1/x $ is NOT continuous at $ x=0 $—it has a vertical asymptote. [[imp: Never extend the graph across the asymptote.]]

questions.prompt: The domain of $ f(x) = \sqrt{x} $ is all $ x \ge $ ___.
hints: Square root of negative is not real.

questions.prompt: What is the range of $ f(x) = \frac{1}{x} $? (use interval notation: (-∞,0)U(0,∞))
Is $ f(x) = \frac{1}{x} $ even, odd, or neither?

challengeCorner.prompt: Describe the domain and asymptotes of $ h(x) = \frac{1}{x+3} + 2 $.
answers: Domain: x ≠ -3; vertical asymptote x=-3, horizontal asymptote y=2
hints: Denominator $ x+3 $ gives vertical asymptote at $ x=-3 $.
The $ +2 $ shifts the horizontal asymptote to $ y=2 $.

blocks.title: 4. Step and Piecewise-Defined Functions
teacherCues: Ask: 'What function looks like a staircase?'
Introduce the greatest integer function and piecewise-defined functions.

discoveryHook.scenario: Parking garage rates: $2 for the first hour, $1 for each additional hour or part thereof. This is a [[kw:step function]]—the cost jumps at each hour mark. The [[kw:greatest integer function]] $ f(x) = \lfloor x \rfloor $ is a classic example, rounding down to the nearest integer.

explanation: A [[kw:step function]] has a graph that looks like a series of steps. The [[kw:greatest integer function]] $ f(x) = \lfloor x \rfloor $ outputs the greatest integer less than or equal to $ x $.
Domain: all real numbers. Range: all integers.
The graph is constant on intervals $ [n, n+1) $ and jumps at each integer.
[[kw:Piecewise-defined functions]] use different formulas for different parts of the domain. Graph each piece on its interval, using open/closed dots at boundaries.
[[imp: For piecewise functions, check the domain conditions to decide which piece to use for a given $ x $.]]

visuals.title: Greatest Integer Function Values
visuals.caption: The greatest integer less than or equal to $ x $; always rounds down.

formulaCard.title: Greatest Integer Function
notes: Domain: all reals; range: all integers.
Graph in dot mode on calculator to avoid connecting the steps.

examples.title: A – Evaluate a step function
examples.prompt: Given $ f(x) = \lfloor x \rfloor + 1 $, find $ f(-1), f(2), f(1.5) $.
steps: $ f(2) = \lfloor 2 \rfloor + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3 $.

examples.title: B – Why use open/closed dots in piecewise graphs?
examples.prompt: Explain why the graph of $ f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x+3, & x \le 1 \\ -x+4, & x > 1 \end{cases} $ has a solid dot at $ (1,5) $ and an open dot at $ (1,3) $.
examples.peerPrompt: Look at the inequality at $ x=1 $.
steps: At $ x=1 $, the condition $ x \le 1 $ applies, so we use $ 2x+3 $ → $ f(1)=5 $. This point is included → solid dot.
The second piece $ -x+4 $ applies only when $ x > 1 $, so at $ x=1 $ it is not included → open dot.
Open and closed dots show which piece includes the boundary point.

examples.title: C – Evaluate piecewise
examples.prompt: $ f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2, & x < 0 \\ x+1, & x \ge 0 \end{cases} $. Find $ f(-2) $ and $ f(0) $.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: The greatest integer function is step-shaped; most graphing utilities connect steps in connected mode. [[imp: Use dot mode to see the true step behavior.]]

questions.prompt: The greatest integer function $ \lfloor x \rfloor $ returns the largest integer ___ than or equal to $ x $.
For the piecewise $ f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x, & x \le 0 \\ x-1, & x > 0 \end{cases} $, find $ f(0) $. (number only)

challengeCorner.prompt: Graph the piecewise function $ f(x) = \begin{cases} x+2, & x < -1 \\ x^2, & -1 \le x \le 1 \\ 3, & x > 1 \end{cases} $. Identify any breaks or jumps.
answers: Break at x = -1 and x = 1; the graph jumps at these points.
hints: Piece 1: line with open dot at $ (-1,1) $.
Piece 2: parabola with closed dots at $ (-1,1) $ and $ (1,1) $. Piece 3: horizontal line with open dot at $ (1,3) $.

blocks.title: 5. Parent Functions Review and Blueprint
teacherCues: Ask: 'Which parent function has a V shape? Which one has a U shape?'
Summarize the library of parent functions and how to recognize them.

discoveryHook.scenario: Think of parent functions as the 'basic shapes' in a toolkit. The absolute value function $ f(x) = |x| $ makes a V; the squaring function makes a U; the cubic makes an S. Once you learn these eight shapes, you can quickly sketch many other functions by applying simple transformations.

explanation: The eight [[kw:parent functions]] are the simplest forms of common function families.
They include: constant, identity, absolute value, square root, squaring, cubic, reciprocal, and greatest integer.
Knowing each one's domain, range, symmetry, intercepts, and general shape is essential for analyzing more complex functions.
Use the blueprint: (1) Recognize the parent family. (2) Note any transformations (shifts, stretches, reflections) that modify the parent. (3) Sketch by starting with the parent and applying changes.
[[imp: Parent functions are the foundation—all other functions in their family are built from them.]]

visuals.title: The Eight Parent Functions
visuals.caption: Memorize these eight shapes—they appear throughout precalculus.

formulaCard.title: Parent Functions Summary
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{Linear, Absolute Value, Square Root, Squaring, Cubic, Reciprocal, Greatest Integer} $$
notes: Each parent is the simplest form of its family.
Transformations (shifts, stretches) are covered in the next section.

examples.title: A – Identify the parent
examples.prompt: What is the parent function of $ g(x) = \sqrt{x-3} + 2 $?
steps: The base operation is the square root.
Parent: $ f(x) = \sqrt{x} $.
The $ -3 $ shifts right 3, $ +2 $ shifts up 2.

examples.title: B – Why learn parent functions?
examples.prompt: Explain how knowing the parent function helps you quickly graph $ h(x) = |x+2| - 3 $.
examples.peerPrompt: Think about starting with the V shape and moving it.
steps: The parent $ f(x) = |x| $ is a V with vertex at $ (0,0) $.
$ x+2 $ inside shifts left 2; $ -3 $ outside shifts down 3.
So the vertex moves to $ (-2,-3) $, and the V shape stays the same.
Without knowing the parent, you'd have to plot many points from scratch.

examples.title: C – Classify a function
examples.prompt: What parent family does $ f(x) = -2(x-1)^3 + 4 $ belong to?
steps: The cube power tells us it's from the cubic family.
Parent: $ f(x) = x^3 $.
It is reflected (negative sign), stretched, and shifted.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: Not every function looks exactly like its parent—shifts, stretches, and reflections change its position and size. [[imp: Focus on the basic shape and the family it belongs to.]]

questions.prompt: The parent function for a V-shaped graph is $ f(x) = |x| $, called the ___ value function.
Which parent function has a vertical asymptote at $ x=0 $? (name: reciprocal, square root, cubic, etc.)
What is the domain of the square root parent function? (use interval notation: [0,∞))

challengeCorner.prompt: Sketch a quick graph of $ f(x) = -|x+4| + 2 $ by identifying the parent, vertex, and direction of opening.
hints: Shift left 4, up 2 → vertex $ (-4,2) $; negative sign flips V downward.
